Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

liberal adjective and noun

in politics

also liberals, liberalism

modern

Levi–Bini p. 38, s.v. liberale (t. polit.)

līberē dē rē pūblicā sentiēns

participle phrase, with sentiō, sentīre

liberal: holding free views about the state

A modern description in classical words; Morgan–Owens and Traupman give no term. Traupman gives optimātēs for the conservatives of ancient Rome (p. 178), but the optimātēs were the men who worked through the senate and the leading families, and the populārēs those who worked through the people’s assemblies (Cic. Sest. 96, Lewis & Short s.v. optimās): methods and alliances, not programmes. Neither is a modern conservative or liberal party, and the words are best not used for them.

Other words

  • līberālis, līberāle — befitting a free man; generous

    avoid · classical · Cic. Off. 1.150 (Lewis & Short)

    A false friend for the political sense: classically worthy of a free man, gentlemanly, kind, and above all generous (Lewis & Short). In that sense it is the right word; the liberal arts are artēs līberālēs (see culture).

See also conservative, party, culture, freedom.

SourcesLewis & Short: liberalis · Lewis & Short: libere · Lewis & Short: sentio · Lewis & Short: optimas · Lewis & Short: popularis

Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 38, s.v. liberale.
